title: Floods don't end when the water goes down
label: 17 November 2026 · Flood response and recovery
summary: The committee heard from people supporting flooded households and farmers, followed by representatives of councils, drainage boards and fire services. Witnesses described lasting damage to health, finances, homes and farmland. They said emergency services often respond well, but warnings can be hard to act on and support becomes less clear once the immediate danger passes. They differed on whether some improvements need new legal duties or better use of existing arrangements, while repeatedly calling for clearer responsibilities, stronger local relationships and more support for recovery.

glossary.definition: The public body responsible for managing flood risk from rivers and the sea in England, among other environmental work.
Groups that bring local public services and other organisations together to plan for and respond to emergencies.
Local public bodies that manage water levels and drainage in areas with particular drainage needs.
A scheme that helps insurers offer flood cover to eligible homes at high risk of flooding.
A responsibility that an organisation is required by law to carry out.
Organisations with the main legal duties to prepare for and respond to emergencies, including councils and emergency services.
Organisations, including utility companies, with duties to co-operate and share relevant information in emergency planning.

chapters.title: The harm that lasts
chapters.takeaway: Flooding can leave people, businesses and farms dealing with costs and distress long after the visible damage is cleared.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What does flooding do to communities beyond the immediate damage?

evidence.quote: I am looking for the whole range of different impacts. There will be business impacts. There will be health impacts, economic impacts, and wellbeing impacts as much as anything else.

turns.speaker: Katia Sanhueza-Pino
turns.text: The visible damage is only a small part of it. Flooding can change a household's or business's life, bringing trauma, anxiety and a long recovery. Even insured people face costs, and help can arrive too late to cover what they must pay upfront. From what we hear, people often don't know where to get support, so communities fill gaps themselves.

evidence.quote: It is important to say that the damage that you see after a flood is the smallest part of a flood event. For communities, it is life-changing. For any household, and for any business as well, it is a life-changing event. It causes trauma and anxiety, and it is a long process of recovery.

From what we hear from people on the ground, there is a lack of co-ordination. There is a lack of specific information and guidance on where they can get support. It is often communities that step up in the response, filling gaps in the formal provision that may be there.

It is a financial impact as well for many households, not just for the uninsured but also for the insured. Also, where there is financial support available, sometimes it arrives too late so there is an upfront cost that people have to face before any grants are made available.

turns.speaker: Paul Tompkins
turns.text: Repeated floods can damage soil for years. In our surveys, farming members say they've spent about £40,000 on average responding to climate events, including floods, over the past decade. Farmers also describe the emotional strain on their families, alongside moving cattle, changing crops and dealing with the bills.

evidence.quote: Also, of course, repeated floods have serious impact on soil degradation and can take many years to recover from.
We survey our members on a regular basis, and they tell us that over the last 10 years, on average, our farming members are spending around £40,000 on responses to climate events, such as flooding.

while they talk to me about the logistics of moving cattle around, of changing cropping rotations or of the financial implications, I don’t need to scratch far below the surface before they start telling me about the emotional impacts of what it is brought to their lives, their families and how they respond.

turns.speaker: Tracey Garrett
turns.text: People tell us they can't sleep when it rains and take turns watching water levels. Insurance often leaves expenses unpaid, and restoring a home can mean time off work. In one community we worked with, homes still hadn't been dried properly 12 years after a flood, and residents were suffering respiratory illnesses.

evidence.quote: They talk about not being able to sleep when it rains. They do shifts to watch the water levels. Home does not feel like home anymore.
Even though they may have insurance, there are a lot of out-of-pocket costs that they never get reimbursed for. They may have to take extensive time off work.
We worked with one community that was 12 years post flood and their homes had not been dried out properly, so they were all suffering with respiratory diseases and illnesses.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Is there enough mental health support for people after a flood?

evidence.quote: The actual level of support that there is for mental health and the wellbeing implications—Tracey in particular, how do you see that?

turns.speaker: Tracey Garrett
turns.text: There isn't much. Research we cited found that even where support existed, only 10% managed to access it. And that fear of rain isn't confined to places with a long history of flooding: it can follow a single flood, or even a near miss.

evidence.quote: There really isn’t that much, to be honest with you. Even if there has been some mental health support, the "stories after the storm" research show that people found it very difficult to access that support with only 10% actually managing to access support.
If you flooded once, it tends to be that that is how you feel about it.
It is just if you have flooded or almost flooded.

turns.speaker: Sarah Dyke
turns.text: Some Somerset farmers have land underwater for months, holding water back from homes farther downstream. Should they be compensated for that?

evidence.quote: For six months, their farmland is underwater. Do you feel that those farmers should be compensated properly, because at the moment what they are doing is taking that rainwater, holding it back from communities further downstream

turns.speaker: Paul Tompkins
turns.text: Yes. If farmers are holding floodwater on their land, they should be adequately compensated.

evidence.quote: in the event that farmers are holding on to flooded water, then they should be adequately compensated for doing so. Absolutely, that is a given.

chapters.title: Warnings people can use
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses wanted clearer, more locally useful warnings and a dependable way to find help without expecting volunteers to do everything.

turns.speaker: Sarah Dyke
turns.text: How could communication improve before, during and immediately after a flood?

evidence.quote: How do you feel that the Government could improve the quality of communications before, during and immediately after a flood event?

turns.speaker: Katia Sanhueza-Pino
turns.text: Flood warnings matter enormously, but they need to say more clearly what people can do and where they can get help. Messages also need to fit the place: storms are putting some communities at risk that weren't at risk before. We must take care not to cause panic by telling people about a danger without giving them useful actions.

evidence.quote: Yes, I think flood warnings are massively important for flooded communities. Nobody would want to be without them
I think it would help if the messaging contained a more actionable and accurate details on where to get information and what to do. However, we always risk that that message will cause panic

With the increase in climate impacts and increased storms, we see a whole range of communities and areas that are now at risk that were not at risk before, so it does need careful targeting and messaging

turns.speaker: Paul Tompkins
turns.text: Farmers need to know what is happening across the area that drains into their local river. I've seen good local planning in Somerset and Lincolnshire. Elsewhere, people managing flood gates may still depend on informal WhatsApp messages about decisions made days earlier. That isn't reliable enough.

evidence.quote: Where I see communication working well is when farmers understand the sensitivities of the catchment in which they farm and, therefore, what the potential implications are going to be, whether that be a flooding or drought event.
I have seen that work well in Somerset. I have seen it work well in Lincolnshire.

communications are still happening through informal WhatsApp groups, where the people who may operate sluice gates are waiting for a call to come through at 9 o’clock in the morning from a decision that has been made two days ago

turns.speaker: Tracey Garrett
turns.text: Community-run monitoring could help, but asking residents to take on more needs funding and support. Where people live also affects the help they get. Some say warnings now lack the local human interpretation they once had, and when flooding starts they don't know whom to contact. Neighbours end up helping neighbours.

evidence.quote: there is a lot that can be done to utilise and work with communities, but none of that comes without investment. What we see when we work with communities is a lot is asked of them, which isn’t particularly well supported
it can be a lottery depending on where you live and the personnel who work at your local agencies
They used to get a human interpretation, so local areas had a much better understanding of whether they were going to flood or not.
neighbours support neighbours. One of the overriding comments that comes back from communities is that they have no idea who to contact.

turns.speaker: Sarah Dyke
turns.text: The Government has introduced Flood Action Online, but not a single phone line for help. Would a phone line matter, particularly for people who struggle to use online services?

evidence.quote: in October the Government introduced the Flood Action Online, but stopped short of implementing a single dedicated phone line for people affected by flooding for access to help.
many of whom may not be able to use those digital services, the lack of a single phone line is obviously going to have an impact on their awareness and their safety.

turns.speaker: Tracey Garrett
turns.text: Yes, one contact point for all kinds of flooding would help. It wouldn't necessarily have to be run by a government agency.

evidence.quote: Having one single point of contact for all flooding would really help, but it does not have to be an agency responsibility. It can be delegated if you will.

turns.speaker: Paul Tompkins
turns.text: A single contact point could collect information and be available at all hours, but it mustn't replace the local agency staff who know the area and can help farmers directly.

evidence.quote: A single point of contact can be helpful because it can be a resource that is available at all times

we must not replace one with the other. I would suggest it is a dual approach. We need one point of contact in order that data is collected in one place, but we must make sure that local farmers are able to access local agency staff too.

turns.speaker: Katia Sanhueza-Pino
turns.text: Flood Action Online helps with awareness and preparation, but says less about getting through recovery. People need consistent, trusted information in one place, backed by local councils with the knowledge and staff to put local plans into action.

evidence.quote: Flood Action Online addresses a lot in terms of awareness of risk and preparedness, but it perhaps falls short on the recovery pathway
one place of contact or a place to receive information that is consistent and co-ordinated would be useful.
that needs to filter down to local authorities that have local knowledge and need resources to activate and mobilise their teams and the plans that they have that are adapted to the local area.

turns.speaker: Tracey Garrett
turns.text: People who've signed up for alerts may still not know when to move their things or what else to do. Warnings can arrive when people are already standing in water; they can also arrive so early that people prepare for a flood that doesn't happen. That's emotionally hard, though failing to warn them could be worse.

evidence.quote: so many people do not know what to do if they get an alert or at what point to take what action.
Some of the feedback that we get about warnings is they either come too late and they are already stood in water, or they come too early.

if they come early, and people go ahead and prepare and they put all their furniture up and they take all the actions that they need to take, and then it does not happen it is a very big emotional burden to carry. However, it is also difficult because if you had not warned them and it came it would have been even worse

turns.speaker: Katia Sanhueza-Pino
turns.text: We particularly need to reach communities that haven't flooded before. And we can't assume every community has people with the time, resources or ability to organise a response. Planning has to account for those differences so vulnerable people aren't left behind.

evidence.quote: It is those communities that are at risk but have never experienced flooding that we need to consider.

a community’s ability to respond and prepare will be different. It depends on the demographics, on the availability of leadership, the ability to volunteer, levels of deprivation and marginalisation, so we cannot assume that all communities have equal capacity to respond.
we need to make sure that we do not leave the most vulnerable behind.

chapters.title: Who helps after the emergency?
chapters.takeaway: Volunteers and emergency services are vital, but witnesses described a difficult handover to prolonged, individual recovery.

turns.speaker: Terry Jermy
turns.text: Are the official local resilience forums working closely enough with the volunteers who get on with helping their neighbours?

evidence.quote: Then we have all of these wonderful people in the community volunteering, just getting on with it in my experience. Do you think there is enough co-ordination between those two distinct groups?

turns.speaker: Tracey Garrett
turns.text: No. It varies by area. Some communities have a relationship with their forum; others find it distant and simply organise locally. Volunteers also need support: flood wardens have told us they've faced abuse for closing flooded roads.

evidence.quote: No. Again, it comes down to where you live and which local resilience forum.

some of the feedback was that communities did not even bother with their local resilience forum because it felt impenetrable, it felt far away and distant, so they just got on with it on a very local level.
I have also spoken to flood wardens who are receiving abuse for closing down roads that are flooded and not necessarily getting the support that they might need as volunteers.

turns.speaker: Katia Sanhueza-Pino
turns.text: Where people want to volunteer, give them training, equipment and the ability to do useful tasks. But volunteers aren't currently official emergency responders, and we must plan for places where there aren't enough people able to volunteer.

evidence.quote: where there is capacity, where there is leadership and where they want to do that, we should equip them with the resources, the training and the powers they can have, but they are not currently responders.

in communities where that capacity isn’t there, we need to prepare for that eventuality and make sure that we take them along with us and invest in emergency planning that addresses their needs as well.

turns.speaker: Paul Tompkins
turns.text: Farmers are often first to notice trouble and want to help. But they may not be able to move a flood defence they hold on their farm because of questions about land access, who controls it or insurance. Those practical barriers need addressing if farmers are to help at the right moment.

evidence.quote: farmers feel curtailed or unable to interject for fear of reprisals, whether that be that they can store flood emergency flood defences on their farms, but might not be able to move them when they can spot that there has been a breach just slightly further up the channel. They are often the first to see it as well.

Land access, so accessing the flood asset that might have been breached. Environment Agency control, so who owns that asset and, therefore, who has response to it. Insurance. There are a multitude of reasons why it might not be appropriate to drive your JCB.

turns.speaker: Henry Tufnell
turns.text: Once the immediate danger has passed, do people know what help is available, and is it enough?

evidence.quote: I want to begin by asking whether you think that communities are efficiently supported following the recovery and whether there is sufficient awareness of the available support that is there for them in that event?

turns.speaker: Katia Sanhueza-Pino
turns.text: No. When the emergency services leave, it often isn't clear who takes over. Recovery is personal and can last months or years. People may need specialist practical, emotional and financial help. Even where grants exist, council staff have to administer them, and delays can leave residents paying for drying equipment or somewhere else to stay.

evidence.quote: No, they are not sufficiently supported in terms of recovery. This is one year on, and this will last for many months, if not years, with their wellbeing still being impacted.
when the blue lights leave, and that opens up a gap as to who takes over the recovery support, with nobody stepping forward to do that. Recovery is so specific and deeply personal and individual
from practical support to wellbeing and emotional support, but also financial support.

Local authorities are often left with the duty to administer the grants, but they do not have extra staff to administer them. That causes a time lag, so that the person who needs it most is left with a gap and has to cover the costs of drying equipment or temporary accommodation.

turns.speaker: Paul Tompkins
turns.text: Reopening roads doesn't mean a farm has recovered. Farmers need to know in advance how the Government decides whether flood recovery money will be available. Some received the 2023–24 fund, but others affected by the same rainfall couldn't access it.

evidence.quote: when roads reopen in order that trucks can reach supermarkets again, that is often perceived as we have resolved the issue, where actually the long-term impacts on food and farming have not necessarily been taken into account.
At the moment we have an unknown vacuum in that it will only be at the discretion of a ministerial decision should any sort of support head our way for an emergency event.
some farmers in some catchments—who still experience the same flooding event due to the same rainfall at the same time—were not able to access that fund.

turns.speaker: Tracey Garrett
turns.text: People often don't know what support exists. Insurance doesn't necessarily make recovery straightforward either: disputes can drag on for a year or two, with residents caught between insurers and repair contractors. I agree that the rules for when recovery grants become available should be clearer.

evidence.quote: I think awareness of any support is very, very low, if there is any support available.
they feature disputes over the type of flooring, these kinds of disputes. They can be about anything, but they go on for a really long time, up to one year, two years
They end up being the one that is going between the contractors and the insurance company, and they are basically project managing the whole thing
I totally agree we need some hard and fast rules about when it is going to be activated

turns.speaker: Tracey Garrett
turns.text: Flood Re helps thousands of households obtain insurance, but it's due to end in 2039. If ordinary insurance hasn't become available to them by then, they could be left without cover. Homes built after 2009 aren't eligible for the scheme, which is especially worrying when new homes are built in higher-risk areas.

evidence.quote: At the moment, the Flood Re scheme supports thousands and thousands of households. When that scheme comes to an end in 2039, that will not be available. The intention is that the market will support the exit of Flood Re from the insurance market. If it does not, that will leave thousands and thousands of people without the ability to get insurance.
any homes built after 2009 are not eligible for the Flood Re scheme. They will not be offered flood insurance necessarily
all the new-build properties that we are putting in areas of higher flood risk will not be able to access flood insurance

chapters.title: Making the response work together
chapters.takeaway: The second panel said emergency teams often work well together, but recovery and co-operation across organisations and areas are less dependable.

turns.speaker: Josh Newbury
turns.text: What gets in the way when public bodies need to respond to a flood together?

evidence.quote: Could you tell us what you see as the main barriers to co-ordination between different public bodies that are responding to flood emergencies?

turns.speaker: Phil Garrigan
turns.text: The immediate emergency response is generally well co-ordinated. We need to practise together beforehand, though. The harder part is handing over responsibility as the response ends: recovery takes much longer and needs more people, money and effort.

evidence.quote: we are pretty effective in how we mobilise resources, how we convene through local resilience forums, and how we prioritise the response.
some of that arrangement should be put in place in advance through the planning and the exercising of such events
the handover of responsibility becomes a little bit more difficult to administer and resource and support in the longer term.
the recovery is significantly longer and requires significantly more time, resource and effort

turns.speaker: Councillor Boughton
turns.text: Local relationships make a big difference. The forums work unevenly, in part because a forum isn't itself a legal body that can require its members to follow one agreed decision. Utility and infrastructure companies also have different emergency-planning duties from councils and emergency services, which can make their input harder to secure.

evidence.quote: the multi-agency arrangements work particularly well where there is an established relationship that has built up, particularly at a local and sometimes at a hyper local level.
Local resilience forums have an effective framework, albeit there are challenges there and there is a patchy nature across the country in terms of their effectiveness.
Because it is not a legal entity you cannot be forced to be part of that collective solution as such.

infrastructure and utilities providers fall as category 2 responders rather than category 1 responders. The outcome of that means that sometimes getting their input, particularly where there is impact on infrastructure, which often is the case, can be more challenging

turns.speaker: Andrew McGill
turns.text: When Wainfleet flooded, drainage boards, the Environment Agency and fire services handled the emergency well. Later, the organisations left to deal with recovery faced their usual rules again. For example, moving water from a field back into a river could be held up by a demand to test it, even while the area was still in difficulty.

evidence.quote: If I think back to the flooding of Wainfleet, which was one event that I was involved in, the internal drainage boards were working round the clock at that point, along with the Environment Agency folks. Then we had this breach and the fire brigades and so on turned up and did an excellent job. The actual emergency was dealt with superbly well

You then shift to the recovery phase and the fire brigade have many more responsibilities, particularly in emergency situations, than staying with that event. Then it is left to the local folks to crack on with.
You can’t put the water from this field back in our main river unless it is tested

turns.speaker: Andrew McGill
turns.text: I'd like the Environment Agency to trust capable internal drainage boards to maintain more watercourses. The agency has stopped maintaining some lower-risk rivers because of costs, but the conditions it places on others doing the work remain demanding. I think much could improve through a change in how the organisations work together, without new legislation for everything.

evidence.quote: there needs to be greater trust and confidence in the abilities of the internal drainage boards within her area.

due to the cost restraints that they face, some of the lower and medium consequence rivers are no longer being maintained, but they still wish to have all the criteria in place for anyone else to go in and maintain it.
I don’t think everything has to be legislated. It can be a cultural change from within the organisation to entrust and empower some of the agencies.

turns.speaker: Councillor Boughton
turns.text: My council has a good working relationship with the Environment Agency because we've built it over time. We need to know promptly when it decides to hold water in a flood-storage area: that protects homes downstream but can cause problems upstream. Larger councils planned in the future may find it harder to keep such local communication working.

evidence.quote: We have a good, long-standing relationship with the Environment Agency
if it is to effectively start impounding at the Leigh flood storage area, then that causes issues with flooding further upstream while also defending downstream.
That is where the communication is critical from the Environment Agency. It has worked in our area because we have spent the time building up those relationships
when local government reorganisation happens and we have bigger councils across the country, what is going to happen is that those communications will become much harder

turns.speaker: Phil Garrigan
turns.text: Fire services still lack a statutory duty to respond to floods. We've sought one for a long time. It would clarify our role in rescue and preparation, and how we hand over to other organisations during recovery.

evidence.quote: the lack of statutory responsibility around flood response, that can have some challenging outcomes at a more local level

For a long time, we have sought to ensure that a statutory duty was imparted on the Fire and Rescue Service in regards to flood response and rescue in the immediate phase, which then allows us to understand our role and responsibility
We cannot do some of the preventative work that we do to support the Environment Agency.

turns.speaker: Phil Garrigan
turns.text: When floods cross local boundaries and several places need help at once, some national co-ordination is needed to decide where fire-service resources should go first.

evidence.quote: Flood is very similar. It crosses boundaries in the same way as wildfires do.
my view is that there is some national co-ordination required about where that resource is allocated.

chapters.title: Paying, preparing and learning
chapters.takeaway: The witnesses raised difficult questions about who pays for repeated floods, whether utilities must do more, and how communities can help improve future responses.

turns.speaker: Helena Dollimore
turns.text: In Hastings, a flood attributed to Southern Water cost the fire service £27,000 to respond to. If a company's failure causes a flood, can the fire service recover its costs from that company?

evidence.quote: That incident was found to have been caused by Southern Water
£27,000 for that incident in response to the FOI request.
it is not as clear to me what the mechanism is by which the water companies pay you back for that. Do you have any comment on that?

turns.speaker: Phil Garrigan
turns.text: As far as I'm aware, there's no way for us to recover costs based on what caused a flood. Fire services responded to 17,000 flood incidents last year, and recovering the cost of those responses is usually very difficult, if possible at all. I would welcome an easier way to claim costs back from a company responsible for an incident.

evidence.quote: There isn’t, as far as I am aware, a mechanism for us to recover the costs in relation to the causal factors linked into a flood in this regard.
the Fire and Rescue Service responded to 17,000 flood incidents last year
More often than not it is very difficult, if at all possible, to recover any of the costs associated with that response.
Yes, I do.

turns.speaker: Councillor Boughton
turns.text: Councils should bring people together after a flood. But water, power and other infrastructure companies should have stronger duties to take part, too. Their failures can cause serious problems, and councils can't always secure their co-operation simply by asking.

evidence.quote: Yes, councils are there to convene and should be convening. That is certainly the expectation.
infrastructure operators and utilities, in our view, should be considered to be part of category 1 responders.
It is very difficult to get engagement.

Unless there is a requirement for infrastructure providers and utility companies to engage with local authorities, to take on board seriously the recommendations that local authorities are bringing forward, then ultimately you are reliant on that good will

turns.speaker: Dr Roz Savage
turns.text: After a flood, should there be a required review involving the agencies and the people who were flooded, so everyone can learn what to do better next time?

evidence.quote: There is not really that opportunity to have a debrief after there has been a flood event to see how things could be handled better the next time between the various different agencies and the communities.
Do you think that a review could and should be a legal requirement to make sure that we learn how to respond more effectively?

turns.speaker: Andrew McGill
turns.text: I'm not sure a review needs to be required by law, but it should be built into the way we work. People in Wainfleet were still meeting agencies about the 2019 flood last week. Some remain worried whenever there's heavy rain, and those conversations help keep attention on protecting them.

evidence.quote: I am not necessarily certain it has to be a legal requirement, but it is certainly something that should be written into something somewhere.

the Wainfleet flooding that I mentioned at the beginning was 2019 and there was a meeting on that last week with members of the community, the local councillors, the Environment Agency and the drainage board
There are still worried people turning up on the banks when there is heavy rainfall because the psychological effect when you have been flooded is long lasting.
It keeps us true to making a difference in sustaining the maintenance throughout the future times rather than drifting away from it.

turns.speaker: Councillor Boughton
turns.text: Councils should review what happened, but doing that while supporting recovery and preparing for the next emergency adds work for already stretched teams. If it becomes a legal duty, councils would need funding for it. Communities also need to see how their feedback changes future plans.

evidence.quote: To do that debrief while at the same time trying to prepare for future incidents creates additional pressure on local resources. If this were to become a statutory duty, then it will not be a surprise for me to turn around and say we need to be funded to deal with that accordingly.
it is very difficult for them to know how much of that has been taken into account when preparing for a future emergency scenario.

turns.speaker: Phil Garrigan
turns.text: Services may review their own actions, but after a significant flood the local resilience forum should bring the organisations together to learn from it. Residents need a voice in that review too: they can tell us whether our response actually worked for them. I'm not convinced that making this a legal duty is essential.

evidence.quote: we may well debrief our own response to a particular set of circumstances. I think the local resilience forum on significant events, and maybe that is something to be defined, would trigger a multi-agency debrief to draw the learning in.
more often than not that is public sector organisations or cat 1 and cat 2 responders coming together to share what they experienced and not necessarily the community itself.
The public should be able to hold the mirror up and comment on our response and how effective it was and that should inform the things that we do in the future.
The high-performing local resilience forums would do exactly what you are describing without a statutory responsibility. I would suggest that maybe that is not a necessity

turns.speaker: Ben Goldsborough
turns.text: Andrew, is the way internal drainage boards get money sustainable? Your boards have to protect low-lying land, but individual projects can need funding from several places.

evidence.quote: The funding had to come through grant in aid funding for flood and coastal erosion risk management projects and environmental statutory funds, plus funding from different bodies such as Norfolk County Council and others. Andrew, do you think the current arrangements in how we fund IDBs is sustainable?

turns.speaker: Andrew McGill
turns.text: The costs can rise sharply: one board's annual electricity bill went from £344,000 to just over £1 million. Funding for flood projects tends to favour places with more homes, while our boards also protect farmland and food production. Applying for a grant can take around 200 hours of work. I'd change both how funding is judged and how hard it is to apply.

evidence.quote: our expend on electricity at one board was £344,000 over a year in 2022-23 and in 2023-24 it was £1,000,063
The grant in aid system, again from an IDB area it is geared for properties and there are not so many properties in those areas.
With regard to obtaining those funds, such as grant in aid, it can take 200 man hours to complete the form
I think it needs an overhaul. I think it needs rebalancing and recognition.

turns.speaker: Councillor Boughton
turns.text: Drainage boards do important work, but the charges councils pay them have risen across the country. Councils can't simply refuse those bills. Without more money coming in, they may have to cut something else to pay them; I don't think that's sustainable.

evidence.quote: levies have increased from £38.9 million in 2022-23 to £54.1 million now.
Of course, we can do absolutely nothing about it other than factor that into our budget-setting process.
We recognise the role that the IDBs do. They perform an important function.
Ultimately, though, I do not think this is sustainable in the long run.
local authorities are having to make cuts elsewhere in order to fund the IDBs.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The law distinguishing organisations with primary emergency duties from those required to co-operate is over 20 years old. Is it time to revisit those responsibilities?

evidence.quote: It is over 20 years since we passed the Civil Contingencies Act.
On the question of category 1 and category 2 responders, is that still working as well or would that benefit from a revisit?

turns.speaker: Phil Garrigan
turns.text: The distinction has been useful because it clarifies roles. A review would be sensible, though, and should look at what is expected of organisations when they practise emergency plans together.

evidence.quote: I still think that works because it defines roles and responsibilities.
Is it worth taking a look at whether it is still fit for purpose? I think that would be sensible
